> When the clouds gathered, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew to the Manasa lake, while one-eighth of the flock flew from the water's edge to the forest of lotuses. Three pairs of swans were seen enjoying themselves in the water, which was lovely with young lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of the flock. || 3 ||

**Word Order:** O young woman! When the clouds gathered, ten times the square root of the swan flock went to the Manasa lake. One-eighth of the flock flew from the water's edge to the forest of lotuses. And three pairs of swans were seen indulging in playful activity in the water, beautiful with young lotus stalks. Then tell me the total number of the flock. || 3 ||

**Meaning:** O dear one, aged sixteen! A group of swans existed. Upon the arrival of the rainy season, ten times the square root <gloss>of the total number</gloss> went to Lake Manasa. One-eighth of the flock flew from the edge of the water to a forest of terrestrial lotuses. And three pairs of swans were seen playing with great affection in the water, adorned with soft lotus stalks. Tell me, how many swans were in that flock? || 3 ||

**Setting-out:** Root-multiplier 10. One-eighth 1/8. Visible <gloss>quantity</gloss> 6. Since it is said that the quantity is joined with its remainder, here, by subtracting one part 1/8, we get 7/8. Dividing the visible quantity by this, the visible quantity becomes 48/7. The root-multiplier becomes 80/7. Half the multiplier 40/7. When squared, this becomes 1600/49. Added to the visible quantity 48/7, the sum is 1936/49. Its square root is 44/7. Joined with half the multiplier 40/7, the squared total number of the flock is 144.

**Detailed Working:** According to the rule mentioned in the previous verse, we subtract one-eighth 1/8 from one, resulting in 1/1 - 1/8 = 7/8, or 8-1/8 = 7/8. We divide the visible quantity 6 by this: 6/1 divided by 7/8 = 6/1 × 8/7 = 48/7. By adjusting the seven, this becomes the visible quantity 48/7. Similarly, we divide the root-multiplier 10 by 7/8: 10/1 divided by 7/8 = 10/1 × 8/7 = 80/7. By adjusting the seven, this becomes the root-multiplier 80/7. Now, considering this visible quantity 48/7 and the root-multiplier 80/7, we perform the calculation according to the method mentioned in the previous verse. That is, half of the root-multiplier is 40/7. We square this to get 1600/49. We add this to the visible quantity 48/7...

Vasudeva is the Supreme Brahman. His embodiment is the Supreme Person; He is the Unmanifest, without attributes, peaceful, beyond the twenty-five elements, and immutable, meaning He is devoid of transformation. || 12 ||

->The Lord, who dwells within <term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>primordial nature</gloss>, pervades both inside and out;<-
->Sankarshana, at the beginning of creation, created the waters and deposited His potency within them. || 13 ||<-

He explains the reason for the impossibility of the pure Brahman being the cause of the world. "Dwells within <term>prakṛti</term>" means He is veiled by <term>māyā</term> <gloss>illusion</gloss>; "pervades both inside and out" means He is the material cause of the world. All these attributes are to be understood as belonging to Sankarshana, who is an aspect of Vasudeva, because he is identical in essence to Vasudeva. Sankarshana, who is an aspect of Vasudeva, first created the waters. In those waters, He deposited His potency, which is a specific type of power. || 13 ||

The omnipresent and experienced Lord Sankarshana entered this <term>prakṛti</term> and first created the waters. Thereafter, He established His own brilliance, in the form of a seed, within those waters. || 13 ||

->That became a golden egg, covered everywhere by darkness;<-
->Within it, the eternal Aniruddha was the first to become manifest. || 14 ||<-

What happened thereafter? That water, combined with His power, became a golden, spherical egg, covered everywhere—inside and out—by darkness. The meaning is that a golden egg was born in the space filled with darkness. Within that golden egg, the eternal Aniruddha, who is an aspect of Vasudeva (Sankarshana being a partial manifestation), was the first to become manifest. He was not "created" in the sense of a new origin, following the doctrine of pre-existing effects <term>satkāryavāda</term>. Just as oil is always present in sesame seeds and is only manifested, not created. || 14 ||

That brilliance in the form of a seed assumed the shape of a golden egg. It was surrounded on all sides by darkness. There (within the egg), the eternal Lord Aniruddha first appeared. || 14 ||

->This Lord is read in the Vedas as <term>Hiraṇyagarbha</term> <gloss>Golden Womb/Germ</gloss>;<-
->He is indeed called <term>Āditya</term> <gloss>the First/Sun</gloss> because of his primordial state, and <term>Surya</term> <gloss>the Sun</gloss> because of his expansion. || 15 ||<-

Now, He states His other names for the better understanding of the people. This Aniruddha, who is a portion of Sankarshana and is endowed with the six qualities of divine majesty, is read in the <term>Chhandas</term> <gloss>Vedas</gloss> as <term>Hiraṇyagarbha</term>, because He dwells in the center of the golden egg. This means that in the Vedas, it is well-known that His other name is <term>Hiraṇyagarbha</term>. Indeed, He is called <term>Āditya</term> because He was the first to be manifested. Due to His expansion—because this world is manifested from Him—He is called <term>Surya</term>.

->"<term>Hiraṇyagarbha</term> existed in the beginning; He was the sole Lord of all beings."<-

This is the Shruti <note>scriptural text</note>. || 15 ||

This is the Lord <term>Hiraṇyagarbha</term> who is mentioned in the Vedas. In the beginning...

When the deity for the 'upanshu' (whispered) sacrifice on the full moon is Agni and Soma, then the verse "Agni-Soma, who today..." serves as the 'anuvakya' (invitatory prayer). This has been indicated in the section titled "The deities have been spoken of" (in the Aitareya Brahmana 1.6). He now recites this second verse.

## Hymn Text

**Agni and Soma, whoever today offers this speech to you two.**
**Grant him great vitality, the growth of cattle, and good horses. 2**

->Pada-patha<-
**Agni-Soma. Who. Today. To you two. This. Speech. Honors.**
**To him. Grant. Good-vitality. Of cows. Growth. Good-horses. 2**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma**, the **sacrificer who today**, in this ritual, **honors this** speech in the form of praise **to you two**, for your sake, **to that** sacrificer, **grant growth** of **cows** or cattle. What kind of growth? **Good vitality**, meaning endowed with excellent power and capability, and **good horses**, meaning endowed with excellent horses. Regarding the form 'gavam' (of cows), although the rule 'savekach' would prescribe an accent on the case ending, the prohibition 'na goshvan savavarnai' maintains the original accent.

->He now recites the third verse.<-

## Hymn Text

**Agni and Soma, he who would offer an oblation to you, he who would perform the preparation of the offering.**
**He shall attain full life, with offspring and great vitality. 3**

->Pada-patha<-
**Agni-Soma. Who. Oblation. Who. To you two. Would offer. Offering-preparation.**
**He. With offspring. Good-vitality. All. Life. Attain. 3**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma, the sacrificer who would offer** an oblation (specifically an oblation of clarified butter) **to you two**, or **he who would offer** a ritual preparation <note>original: "havishkritim"</note> made with offerings like the 'charu' (boiled rice) and 'purodasha' (sacrificial cake), **he**, the sacrificer, **shall attain** or reach **all** (the entirety of) **his life**, endowed with **offspring** (such as sons and grandsons) and **good vitality**. Regarding the form 'ahutim' (oblation), the root 'hu' (to sacrifice) with the suffix 'ktin' results in the retention of the original accent of the 'gati' (preverb/particle). 'Dashat' comes from the root 'dash' (to give), taking the 'at' augment in the 'let' (subjunctive) mood. Because it is linked to the relative pronoun 'ya', it does not undergo the 'nighata' (loss of accent). In 'havishkritim', where the 'havis' (offering) is the 'kriti' (doing or preparation), the rule of 'bahuvrihi' compound causes the first member to retain its original accent.

# Because of meditating on the Supreme, its powers are obscured; from that, indeed, come the soul's bondage and liberation. || 3.2.5 ||

|| 3.2.5 ||

It might be argued: the individual soul <term>jiva</term> is merely a part of the Supreme Self <term>para-atman</term>, like a spark from a fire. In that case, just as a fire and its sparks possess the same power of burning and illumination, the individual soul and the Lord <term>Ishvara</term> should both possess the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Consequently, the soul would be capable of creating chariots and other objects in a dream through the mere power of its will <term>sankalpiki</term>. To this, we reply: while it is true that the individual soul and the Lord have a part-and-whole relationship, the fact that the soul possesses qualities contrary to those of the Lord is a matter of direct perception. Does the soul then lack the qualities of the Lord entirely? No, it is not that they are entirely absent; they exist, but are obscured by the obstruction of ignorance <term>avidya</term> and the like. This obscured power only manifests in a creature who, while meditating on the Supreme Lord and exerting the mind, has cleansed away the darkness—much like the power of vision, obscured by cataracts, is restored by the potency of medicine—and this happens only to those who have become perfected through the grace of the Lord, not to all creatures by nature. Why is this? Because from that, from the Lord as the cause, depend the bondage and liberation of this soul; bondage arises from the lack of knowledge of the Lord’s nature, and liberation arises from the knowledge of that nature. The scripture also says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the fading of afflictions, birth and death cease. Through meditation on Him, in the third state at the dissolution of the body, one attains universal sovereignty and becomes fulfilled" <note>This refers to the Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.11</note>, and so on.

# Or because of the connection to the body, that too. || 3.2.6 ||

|| 3.2.6 ||

Why then does the individual soul, while being a part of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty obscured? It is logical that knowledge and sovereignty should remain un-obscured, just as burning and illumination are in a spark of fire. We answer: this is true; however, that obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occurs because of the connection to the body—the connection to the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the experience of objects. There is an analogy for this: just as the power of burning and illumination in a fire, though inherent, is obscured when it is contained within a piece of wood, or when it is covered by ashes, in the same way, the obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty arises from the connection to the limiting adjuncts <term>upadhi</term>—the body, name, and form—which are set up by ignorance, and from the confusion caused by distinguishing the soul from these. The word "or" <term>va</term> is used to ward off the doubt that the soul is distinct from the Lord. But, one might ask, could the soul be something other than the Lord, precisely because its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured; why posit a connection to the body? We reply: no, it is not reasonable for the soul to be other than the Lord. The scripture begins with "That Deity thought" <note>Referring to Chandogya Upanishad 6.3.2</note> and continues with "having entered by this individual soul as the self," referring to the soul with the word "Self" <term>atman</term>. Furthermore, it instructs the soul in its lordship, saying, "That is the Truth, that is the Self, That Thou Art, O Shvetaketu." Therefore, the soul is non-different from the Lord, and it is only because of the connection to the body that its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured. Consequently, the creation of chariots and such in a dream by the soul's will does not hold. If the creation of chariots in a dream were truly a matter of will, no one would ever experience an unpleasant dream, for no one wills an unpleasant thing. Regarding the argument that the scriptural mention of the waking state proves the reality of the dream state, such a comparison does not imply equal reality, as that would contradict the soul's nature as self-luminous, and the scripture itself shows the absence of actual chariots in a dream. Such a comparison is intended to show that the dream is like the waking state because it is caused by latent impressions <term>vasana</term> from the waking state. Therefore, it is established that the dream is mere illusion <term>maya-matram</term>.

# Its absence is in the channels, according to scripture, and in the Self. || 3.2.7 ||

The Section on Its Absence || 3.2.7 ||

The dream state has been examined; now the deep sleep state <term>sushupti</term> is being examined. There are these scriptural passages concerning deep sleep: in one place, it is heard, "When a person is thus asleep, fully integrated and serene, not knowing any dream, then he is asleep in the channels <term>nadi</term>." In another place, specifically mentioning the channels, it is heard, "Having glided through them, he rests in the pericardium <term>puritat</term>." Similarly, in another place, after mentioning the channels, it says, "He remains in them when he is asleep and does not see any dream, and then he becomes unified in the Vital Breath <term>prana</term> alone." Likewise, in another place, "He rests in that space which is within the heart." In another, "O Saumya, at that time he becomes united with the Being; he has attained his own Self." And also, "Embraced by the Prajna-Self, he knows nothing external or internal."

A doubt arises here: are these—the channels and the others—separate places of deep sleep independent of each other, or are they a single place of deep sleep, depending on one another? What is the conclusion? They are separate, because, since they have the same purpose, there is no interdependence between them.

<summary>Shankara explains that the soul's limited knowledge is an effect of its identification with the body, which obscures its inherent divine nature. He then transitions to the analysis of deep sleep, questioning whether various scriptural locations for this state—the channels, the heart, the pericardium, or the Supreme Being—are independent or unified.</summary>
<keywords>Jiva, Ishvara, Avidya, Upadhi, Obscuration, Deep Sleep, Sushupti, Nadi, Puritat, Prana</keywords>

## Thence comes speed of mind, the state of bodilessness, and mastery over the primal cause. ॥ 48 ॥

Speed of mind is the attainment of incomparable motion for the body. The state of bodilessness is the attainment of the functions of the sense organs—independent of the body—in relation to desired locations, times, and objects. Mastery over the primal cause is the control over all modifications of nature. These three accomplishments are called "honey-like" <note>This term, <term>madhupratīkā</term>, refers to a stage of yogic attainment where the fruits of practice become sweet or pleasant.</note>. These are attained through the mastery of the five forms of the senses. ॥ 48 ॥

## For one established solely in the discriminative discernment between the intelligence and the pure self, there arises sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience. ॥ 49 ॥

For one whose intelligence has been cleansed of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> <gloss>activity/passion</gloss> and <term>tamas</term> <gloss>inertia/darkness</gloss>, who is established in supreme clarity, who remains in the state of total self-mastery, and who is fixed solely in the discriminative discernment between the intelligence <note>The <term>buddhi-sattva</term>, the purest form of cognitive faculty.</note> and the pure self <note>The <term>puruṣa</term> or conscious witness.</note>, there arises sovereignty over all states of existence. The <term>guṇas</term> <gloss>constituents of nature</gloss>, which comprise all, are determinative...

---

Regarding the accomplishments <note>attained</note> through the mastery of the five forms of the senses, he says: **"Thence comes speed of mind, the state of bodilessness, and mastery over the primal cause."** The state of bodilessness is the instrument-like functioning of the senses that are <note>otherwise</note> independent of the body. Location is <note>places like</note> Kashmir and so on. Time is the past and so on. Object is the subtle <note>elements</note> and so on. Through the mastery of the senses in their connection <note>to these objects</note>, there arises control over all modifications of nature; this is mastery over the primal cause. These accomplishments are called "honey-like" by those learned in the science of Yoga.

One might ask: "If there is mastery over the senses, the senses with their objects may be under control, but what follows for their causes, like the primal cause?" He replies: **"These are..."** This refers to the mastery of the five forms of the instruments, that is, the senses, such as the act of grasping. The meaning is this: these accomplishments are not merely from the mastery of the sense organs alone, but from the mastery of <note>their</note> five forms, which include their causes, beginning with the primal cause. ॥ 48 ॥

He now indicates the secondary manifestations of that discriminative discernment between the intelligence and the pure self—the object for which those forms of <term>saṃyama</term> <gloss>concentrated meditation</gloss>, which are the causes of knowledge, action, and lordship, are performed, either directly or indirectly through the faith produced by the realization of one's own accomplishments: **"For one established solely in the discriminative discernment between the intelligence and the pure self, there arises sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience."** Through the removal of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term>, clarity arises. From that, <note>there arises</note> the supreme state of self-mastery. The mind, <note>which is</note> intelligence, was previously overwhelmed by <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term> and was therefore not under control. Upon the pacification of those <note>impurities</note>, it becomes subject to the control of the yogi who has attained mastery. In that state of mastery, for the yogi who is fixed solely in the discernment between the intelligence and the pure self, there arises sovereignty over all states of existence. He explains this: **"The constituents of nature, which comprise all..."**

<margin>Commentary by Su</margin>
If one studies without knowing the Way, knowledge and sight increase daily, but there is no way to unify them; this inevitably leads to a burden. Confucius said, "When hearing much, select the good and follow it; when seeing much, remember it. This is the second level of knowledge." If one truly knows the Way, one looks at falsehood as false. If one acts, it is not without a single thought of deception. Removing deception and returning to one's nature is what is meant by "decrease." When someone asked Confucius, "Do you consider me one who learns much and remembers it?" he replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said, "No. I unify it with one thread." To forget the heart in order to return purely to one's nature is "decrease." If one does not stop at forgetting the heart and returning to one's nature, but proceeds to forget even this, then the heart is pure and the nature is restored without remainder. Then, one removes the "acting," and one does not fail to reach "non-action." People all have desires to take hold of the world and the reasoning of things. Thus, they create affairs and seek them. When the heart manifests externally, things resent it; thus, it is difficult and cannot be attained. The sage practices non-action; thus, there are no affairs. When his heart manifests externally, things are at peace. Even if he does not take hold of the world and its reasoning, and yet handles them, the reasoning of the world is then compliant and peaceful.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin>
Learning is for those who have not yet heard of the Way. Because those who have not heard of the Way seek it, they cannot help but be extensive; hence, it is said, "Increase." Practicing the Way is for those who have already heard of the Way. Because those who have already heard of the Way practice it, they cannot help but be in non-action; hence, it is said, "Decrease." To say "decrease and decrease again" means one has not yet avoided having action. To reach the point of forgetting even the act of decreasing, one arrives at non-action. Non-action means to be silent and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" means to respond and penetrate the causes of the world. To be in non-action and arrive at the ultimate non-action is what is called "the constant." If study has no worry, it is called spirit. The function of spirit is what is called the Way. Who can participate in this ultimate spirit? Looking at it this way, one knows that to take the world, one must always use non-action. If one uses action, one is not enough to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin>
Only when there is nothing one does not know can one speak of learning; thus, learning wishes to increase daily. Only when there is nothing one does not do can one speak of the Way; thus, the Way wishes to decrease daily. However, "increase" can be pursued through advancement, while "decrease" is perhaps difficult to force. Only the extremely bright can suddenly cast off their attachments and arrive at the ground of non-action. Thus, they can do nothing that is not done, and their application in the world is inexhaustible and abundant.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai</margin>
Learning is the means to seek knowledge; thus, it increases daily. Practicing the Way is the means to remove deception; thus, it decreases daily. If knowledge is not extreme, the decrease is not complete; thus, "increasing daily" is the ground for "decreasing daily." If one decreases and decreases again, deception is removed and the true is complete, then there is non-action. Once one reaches non-action, whatever is done is never "not-non-action." This is not something that can be easily discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When one arrives at the ultimate non-action, even though the world is vast, one unifies it with a single thread. If one creates affairs where there are none, one is hard-pressed. If even a single thing from before is still tangled and erroneous, how much more so for the multitude of things in the world?

The sage has no constant heart. He takes the heart of the common people as his heart. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good, so that virtue becomes good. To those who are trustworthy, I am trustworthy; to those who are not trustworthy, I am also trustworthy, so that virtue becomes trustworthy. 19. Then Ragâ, the daughter of Māra, spoke this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
Having severed the craving that flows like a swarm of bees,
many beings will surely pass over.
Truly, this homeless one
will lead many people away to the King of Death.

20. The great heroes, the Tathâgatas <gloss>those who have thus come/gone</gloss>, lead by the true teaching <term>saddhamma</term>.
Since they are led by the teaching, what jealousy can there be for those who understand?

21. Then Taṇhâ, Arati, and Ragâ, the daughters of Māra, approached the place where Māra the Evil One was.

22. Māra the Evil One saw Taṇhâ, Arati, and Ragâ, the daughters of Māra, coming from afar. Seeing them, he addressed them in verses:
Fools, you try to crush a mountain with lotus stalks,
you dig at a mountain with your fingernails, you chew on it with iron teeth.
You seek a foothold in the abyss, bumping your head against a rock.
You collide with a stump with your breast, trying to shake Gotama.

23. Taṇhâ, Arati, and Ragâ arrived, shining brightly.
The Teacher dispelled them there, just as the wind disperses a tuft of cotton.

Aṅguttara-Nikāya. XI.

Just as, Venerable Sir, a duster <note>original: "rajoharaṇa" - a cloth used for cleaning dust</note> wipes away both what is clean and what is unclean, what is covered in excrement, what is covered in urine, what is covered in saliva, what is covered in pus, and what is covered in blood, and the duster is not troubled, ashamed, or disgusted by it: in this way, Venerable Sir, I dwell with a mind like a duster: vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill-will. Should there be anyone, Venerable Sir, who has not established mindfulness of the body, he might offend a fellow practitioner here and depart on his travels without seeking forgiveness.

Just as, Venerable Sir, a young outcaste boy or girl, wearing a loincloth <note>original: "kaḷopihattho" - holding a bowl or bundle</note> and carrying a vessel, enters a village or town having established a humble mind: in this way, Venerable Sir, I dwell with a mind like a young outcaste: vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill-will. Thus, indeed, the Supreme is taught as being beyond all these, so it is reasonable; it is not the case that superiority is taught for each of them individually. Why? Because there is no purpose. For no purpose is seen or heard when superiority is understood in the others. However, when the Person <term>puruṣa</term> is understood as being beyond the senses and so on, and beyond the totality of all objects, a purpose is seen: the attainment of liberation <term>mokṣa</term>. And so the Shruti says, "Having realized this, one is liberated from the mouth of death" (Katha 3.15). Moreover, by forbidding others and by the word "limit" <term>kāṣṭhā</term>, it shows reverence for the subject of the Person; it shows that the flow from the beginning to the end exists for the sake of the realization of the Person—that is, "for the sake of the narrative." The meaning is that this narrative is for the sake of true knowledge <term>samyag-darśana</term>. For this narrative is taught precisely for the sake of true knowledge, and not that the narrative itself is the primary goal. (14)

**And because of the word "Self" (Atman). (15)**

This is another reason why the mention of the flow of senses and so on is for the sake of the realization of the Person. Because "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth, but is seen by the subtle, sharp intellect of those who see the subtle" (Katha 3.12), it speaks of the previously mentioned Person as the "Self." Therefore, it is understood that the others are not intended to be the "Self," and it shows that He alone is difficult to know and to be known by the refined mind. For the sake of knowing Him, it provides the narrative: "The wise person should restrain speech in the mind" (Katha 3.13). That has been explained in "Even the inferential one is in some" (Brahma Sutra 1.4.1). Thus, in many ways...

**Bhamati**
"That is the limit," so says the Veda. By the indicator of the negation of others and the indicator of the superiority of all beings, it shows that the purport is in the Person. It shows that the statement of the superiority of each subsequent one over the previous one is for that purpose, he says, "Moreover." He applies the sutra to the fact that the words beginning with 'artha' are for the sake of meditation, and the previous ones are for the sake of seeing the Person, because there is no purpose in themselves: "For the sake of the narrative" (14). "And because of the word 'Self'." Moreover, because of the consistency of the opening and the conclusion, such as "That supreme state of Vishnu, beyond the Person, there is nothing," there is a certainty of a single sentence aimed at a single Person who is the goal. Therefore, the assumption of sentence splitting or purpose splitting is not reasonable due to the fault of over-elaboration, he says, "Moreover" (15).

**Nyaya Nirnaya**
"Why?" Because the purport is the object of knowledge, and because of the lack of results in knowing the others and their superiority, he considers "because there is no purpose." How is the statement of the lack of purpose made? Doubting whether the result is established by logic, by the scripture, or by both, he rejects the first. He replies to the second: "And it is heard." Because the context is seen to be focused on the reality of the object, it is not suitable to be focused on the injunction of worship. If it is focused on the knowledge of the ultimate reality of the highest Person, then, since the doctrine of the senses is for the sake of other human goals, the focus cannot be on each individual, meaning there is no establishment of focus on each. The knowledge of the superiority of the Person is also not fruitful if it is mere inference of superiority over the senses, but why is there a causality of human purpose? He states, "However, in the Person," because of being the subject of the infinite, characterized by the absence of meaning, the desire for superiority in the Person is established by experience as having no destruction. He says, "it is seen." To one who differs in the experience of the learned regarding the fruits of seeing the superiority of the Person, he provides the Shruti: "And so." He says, "Moreover," because the entire context is focused on the knowledge of the Person. By the indicator of the negation "beyond the Person," by the word "limit" meaning boundary, and by the indicator of superiority, the Veda shows reverence for the subject of the Person. The mention of the flow from the beginning to the end is the statement of the superiority of each subsequent one over the previous one. Because there is no injunction of meditation here, how is the knowledge of the supreme Person for the sake of meditation heard? Doubting this, he explains the part of the sutra: "For the sake of the narrative." Even the knowledge of the unqualified Brahman is for the sake of meditation because it is situated in Brahman. He objects to the contradiction with the Shruti "Then, that," and says, "true knowledge" (14). He gives another reason for the Person being the one taught as superior to all: "And because of the word 'Self'." He explains the word "ca" in the sutra: "And from this also." Clarifying that, he parses the word "Atman": "That which..." He prevents the doubt that the non-shining of the Self is natural: "But is seen." He says "the mentioned," because of the "Atman" in that very Shruti. He states the intended meaning by explaining the word in the sutra: "Therefore." He states the means for the remaining previous purpose: "Of that." He states the purport of the latter part: "Refined..." He states another reason indicated by the word "ca": "That." He objects that only the regulation of speech and so on is implied in the mantra, not the injunction of meditation, and says, "That has been explained." Because the unknown meaning is for the sake of the repetition, the difficulty of knowing the Self is explained in the scripture, and because the others are easy to understand, the statement of their superiority is also meant for the purport. Thus, the opening and conclusion...

**Shridhara Swami’s Commentary**—If You grant liberation only to those who are devoted, and not to those who are not, does this mean that You have partiality born of attachment or aversion? Even while this is true, those who worship Me, they are devotees, and they exist in Me, and I in them, in the capacity of one who shows grace. Whoever, even a person of very evil conduct like Ajamila and others, if they worship Me having no other desire, having experienced the dawning of good fortune, they serve Me; such a person, though formerly unrighteous, should be considered righteous. **Shridhara Swami’s Commentary**—Furthermore, showing that the influence of devotion to Me is inconceivable, He says, "Even if..." If a person of extremely evil conduct does not worship other deities but worships only Me, Sri Narayana, then he should be considered righteous, indeed superior. Because he has made the right resolution: "I will be fulfilled by worshiping the Supreme Lord alone," he has formed a good determination. <note>30</note>

**Madhusudana Saraswati’s Commentary**—From this very right resolution, having abandoned his evil conduct—

> He quickly becomes a righteous soul, and attains eternal peace. 
> O son of Kunti, proclaim that My devotee never perishes. <note>31</note>

Though one may have been unrighteous for a long time, by the greatness of devotion to Me, one quickly becomes a righteous soul, one whose mind follows the path of dharma, meaning one who abruptly abandons evil conduct and becomes virtuous. Furthermore, one attains eternal peace—the cessation of the desire for sense objects—and attains it completely due to deep detachment. But what if My devotee, not having abandoned the evil conduct practiced before, does not become a righteous soul, and thus he indeed perishes? "The body gains strength" means the body becomes strong. By the method mentioned here, which is the method of practice, the lord of yogis, who is like a king among yogis, truly becomes free from all disturbances on the face of the earth. The logic follows that every statement is provided with certainty, meaning the fruit that has been described is indeed true. || 56 ||

The author describes <term>Shitali Kumbhaka</term>. "With the tongue" means that by extending the tongue out of the lips, resembling the lower beak of a bird, one should draw in the air and perform an inhalation. "Called <term>Shitali</term>" is a term used to indicate the well-known name. This <term>kumbhaka</term> removes them entirely. The word <term>kumbhaka</term> is feminine here.

○ III. Manifesting the characteristics of the aforementioned dependent origination, which is the sentence concerning the defiled mind.

○ 1. The Heading.
The defiled mind has six types.

○ 2. The Inquiry.
What are the six?
Within the six, each has two parts: the first is the obstruction, and the latter is the remedy.

○ 3. The Explanation.
Regarding these six defilements, they are matched in reverse order to the six coarse characteristics. The first four, and the latter three subtle ones—as stated in the *Awakening of Faith Commentary*, Volume 1, same as this.
The first item here corresponds to the third and fourth of the coarse ones, thus there are only six. Therefore, I borrow these names to categorize these six.

○ First, the characteristic of attachment and calculation regarding names.

1. The "attachment-correspondence defilement." It relies on the liberation of the <term>erjen</term> <gloss>two vehicles: Shravakas and Pratyekabuddhas</gloss> and the stage of correspondence with faith, where it is far removed. This corresponds to the third and fourth of the six coarse characteristics. It is also the meaning of what is increased by the view and attachment afflictions of the consciousness mentioned above, and it is also the characteristic of grasping and attachment in the discrimination among the four characteristics mentioned above. It is called "defiled" because the coarse mind attaches externally to objects, corresponding to the objective realm and staining pure practice. "Liberation of the two vehicles" refers to the stage of no-more-learning, where view and practice afflictions are completely departed from. "Correspondence with faith" refers to the ten stages of understanding <note>the *Shi-jie*</note> and beyond, where the root of faith is perfected and never retrogresses. Thus, it is named "correspondence with faith." The *Treatise on the Ten Stages* <term>Dashabhumika Sutra</term> says that before the stages, it is collectively called the stage of faith-practice. The *Mahayana-sutralamkara* <gloss>Treatise on the Adornment of the Mahayana</gloss> also shares this view. This Bodhisattva

This is not regarding the latent tendencies <term>anusaya</term> <gloss>latent afflictions</gloss> retaining the confusion. The *Mahayana-samparigraha* <gloss>Summary of the Mahayana</gloss> says: "If one does not sever the upper mind, then one is no different from an ordinary person; if one does not retain the seeds of confusion, then one is no different from the two vehicles." If one refers to the Initial Teaching <term>Shijiao</term>, only from the first stage onward is retaining confusion discussed, as other treatises state. This Bodhisattva not only severs the four dwellings and attachment to human-self, but also partially severs the dwelling of ignorance. ### Section 8: The Birth of Merit through the Teaching

Subhuti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the three-thousand-great-thousand worlds with the seven treasures and use them for charity, would the merit obtained by this person be great?

Subhuti replied: Very great, World-Honored One! Why? Because this merit is not the nature of true merit. It is for this reason that the Tathagata speaks of the merit as being great.

If, however, there is someone who accepts and upholds even a four-line verse of this sutra and explains it to others, their merit would be even greater. Why?
